```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5
)
has_cdtr <- requireNamespace("cdtr", quietly = TRUE) &&
  "cdt_locate" %in% getNamespaceExports("cdtr")
mdim_file <- if (requireNamespace("gdalraster", quietly = TRUE) &&
                 "mdim_read" %in% getNamespaceExports("gdalraster") &&
                 isTRUE(gdalraster::gdal_formats("netCDF")$multidim_raster)) {
  system.file("extdata", "mdim_small.nc", package = "gdalraster")
} else ""
```

```{r setup}
library(ximage)
```

An image is two dimensions, but the data we read from Zarr, NetCDF and the
GDAL multidimensional API usually has more: time, depth, band, ensemble
member. And its coordinates aren't always a tidy extent: latitude may run
south to north, spacing may be irregular, or the grid may be curvilinear. This
vignette covers how ximage draws those, and how it draws triangle and quad
meshes with the same colour mapping.

## Arrays: one slice at a time

Here is a small (lon, lat, time) array, in the layout `zaro::zaro_array()`
gives for a C-order Zarr array of shape (time, lat, lon): the dimensions
reversed, named through `dimnames`. Its latitude runs south to north.

```{r array}
nlon <- 61; nlat <- 87; nt <- 6
lon <- seq(140, 152, length.out = nlon)
lat <- seq(-45, -28, length.out = nlat)
v <- t(volcano[nlat:1, ])  ## (lon, lat), stored south to north
a <- array(c(v, v * 0.96, v * 0.92, v * 0.88, v * 0.84, v * 0.8),
           c(nlon, nlat, nt),
           dimnames = list(lon = NULL, lat = NULL, time = NULL))
o <- ximage(a, coords = list(x = lon, y = lat), asp = 1)
```

The spatial dimensions were found by name, the first time step was drawn
north up (the rows were reversed because the latitudes increase), and the
message says how to draw the others. Use `slice` for another time step and
the returned `zlim` to keep the colours comparable (values outside `zlim`
are drawn as `na.col`):

```{r slice}
ximage(a, coords = list(x = lon, y = lat), slice = list(time = 6),
       zlim = o$zlim, asp = 1)
```

`xslices()` lists the slices (reading only metadata, so it is cheap for
lazy arrays), and `xpanels()` draws several with one colour scale:

```{r panels, fig.height = 5}
head(xslices(a))
xpanels(a, coords = list(x = lon, y = lat), asp = 1)
```

Without dimension names the first two dimensions are rows and columns, as for
any R matrix. A third dimension of 2 to 4 is taken as grey/alpha, RGB or RGBA,
as it always has been, and anything more is slices. Set the spatial
dimensions with `xy` when the names aren't recognised, and select 3 or 4
indices along one dimension for a colour composite, e.g.
`slice = list(band = c(4, 3, 2))`.

Only the slice drawn is read, with `[`, so a lazy `zaro::zaro_array()` (or
any altarr array) fetches only the chunks that slice needs.

### GDAL multidimensional reads

`gdalraster::mdim_read()` returns a flat vector with a `gis` attribute
describing every dimension and its coordinates. ximage uses those
coordinates (here the latitudes run north to south so no flip is needed),
applies the scale and offset, and labels the slice with its decoded time:

```{r mdim, eval = nzchar(mdim_file)}
t2m <- gdalraster::mdim_read(mdim_file, "/t2m")
ximage(t2m, asp = 1, slice = list(time = 3))
xtext(t2m, add = TRUE, slice = list(time = 3))
xslices(t2m)
```

## Coordinates

`coords = list(x = , y = )` places the image by coordinates instead of an
extent. A vector with one value per cell gives cell centres, one more value
gives cell edges (as CF bounds variables do). Regular spacing becomes an
extent, irregular spacing is drawn cell by cell:

```{r irregular}
x <- cumsum(c(0, rep(1, 30), rep(3, 30)))[1:61]  ## spacing changes
y <- seq(0, 86)
ximage(volcano, coords = list(x = x, y = rev(y)), asp = 1)
xcontour(volcano, coords = list(x = x, y = rev(y)), add = TRUE)
```

Matrices give curvilinear coordinates, one per cell (centres) or one more in
each direction (corners). Cells are drawn as quads, and `xcontour()` and
`xtext()` follow them:

```{r curvilinear}
cx <- outer(1:87, 1:61, function(i, j) j + i / 10)
cy <- outer(1:87, 1:61, function(i, j) -i + j / 20 + sin(j / 8) * 4)
ximage(volcano, coords = list(x = cx, y = cy), asp = 1)
xcontour(volcano, coords = list(x = cx, y = cy), add = TRUE)
```

Because corners can be anything, they can be projected. Here the corners of
the global `topo` grid go through an orthographic projection written in
plain R; corners on the far side of the globe are `NA` and their cells are
dropped:

```{r projected, fig.height = 5}
ortho <- function(lon, lat, lon0 = 147, lat0 = -42) {
  rad <- pi / 180
  lon <- lon * rad; lat <- lat * rad; lon0 <- lon0 * rad; lat0 <- lat0 * rad
  cosc <- sin(lat0) * sin(lat) + cos(lat0) * cos(lat) * cos(lon - lon0)
  x <- cos(lat) * sin(lon - lon0)
  y <- cos(lat0) * sin(lat) - sin(lat0) * cos(lat) * cos(lon - lon0)
  x[cosc < 0] <- NA
  y[cosc < 0] <- NA
  list(x = x, y = y)
}
nr <- nrow(topo); nc <- ncol(topo)
glon <- matrix(seq(-180, 180, length.out = nc + 1), nr + 1, nc + 1, byrow = TRUE)
glat <- matrix(seq(90, -90, length.out = nr + 1), nr + 1, nc + 1)
p <- ortho(glon, glat)
op <- par(mar = rep(0, 4))
ximage(topo, coords = list(x = matrix(p$x, nr + 1), y = matrix(p$y, nr + 1)),
       asp = 1, axes = FALSE, col = hcl.colors(96, "Earth"))
par(op)
```

## Meshes

`xmesh()` draws triangle and quad meshes, filled by a value on the vertices
or the faces, with the colour arguments of `ximage()`. It recognises
triangulations from cdtr, RTriangle and laridae, rgl 'mesh3d' objects (from
quadmesh, anglr, textures) and bare vertices with an index of faces.

```{r mesh-bare}
## volcano's cells as a quad mesh
xy <- cbind(rep(0:61, each = 88), rep(87:0, 62))
i <- rep(seq_len(61), each = 87); j <- rep(seq_len(87), 61)
quads <- cbind((i - 1) * 88 + j, i * 88 + j, i * 88 + j + 1, (i - 1) * 88 + j + 1)
xmesh(xy, index = quads, value = as.vector(volcano), asp = 1)
```

A constrained triangulation from cdtr, with a hole, filled by a value at
each vertex. The default "polygon" method gives each face the mean of its
vertices; `method = "raster"` locates every pixel of the plot in the mesh and
interpolates across its triangle, which is smooth and costs pixels rather
than faces:

```{r mesh-cdtr, eval = has_cdtr, fig.height = 3.5}
ring <- function(r, n = 60) {
  a <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = n + 1)[-1]
  cbind(cos(a), sin(a)) * r
}
pts <- rbind(ring(1), ring(0.4))
s0 <- c(1:60, 60 + 1:60)
s1 <- c(c(2:60, 1), 60 + c(2:60, 1))
tri <- cdtr::cdt_triangulate(pts[, 1], pts[, 2], s0 = s0, s1 = s1,
                             max_area = 0.003, erase = "holes")
z <- sin(tri$P[, 1] * 4) * cos(tri$P[, 2] * 4)
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(2, 2, 1, 1))
xmesh(tri, value = z, border = "grey30", asp = 1)
xmesh(tri, value = z, method = "raster", segments = TRUE, asp = 1)
par(op)
```

Faces with a vertex that isn't finite are dropped, so a projected mesh can
mark vertices that fail with `NA`, just as for the projected image above.
